titles.391: Annotatio II §.VI open: SUBTILIOR first author — not Berengar but Ascelinus (Cave vs Bayer/Guitmund)
titles.392: Annotatio II §.VI: Ascelinus follows Paschasius on corporal presence, yet defends coexistence not conversion
titles.393: Annotatio II §.VI: Letter to Berengar — altar bread/wine UNIATUR to the virgin-born body

latin.391: §. VI. POSTERIORIS seu SUBTILIORIS CONSUBSTANTIATIONIS Autor primus non Berengarius est, ex mera incertitudine & aliena relatione, à Guitmundo habitus, quem cæcum ducem secutus est Bajerus Disput. de Impan. num. 15. 16; Sed ASCELINUS, MONACHUS quidam, Wilhelmo Caveo memoratus, multis verò, ut & Bajero ignoratus.
latin.392: Ascelinus enim, in Epistola ad Berengarium ipsum, per Dacherium ex antiquis membranis Abbatiæ Casalis Benedicti, editâ, etiamsi confiteatur, se Paschasii sententiam sequi (nempe quantum ad corporalem carnis Christi praesentiam in sacramento attinet) tamen de pane consecrato & modo praesentiae corporis Christi in Eucharistia longè aliter, ac ille, scribit, non Conversionem panis in Corpus Christi, sed tamen ad minimum Coëxistentiam Corporis cum pane benedicto, defendens.
latin.393: Verba ejus hæc sunt: Neque vero mirari vel diffidere debemus, Deum facere posse ut hoc quod in Altari consecratur (nempe panis & vinum) virtute Spiritus Sancti & ministerio sacerdotis, UNIATUR corpori illi, quod ex Maria Virgine Redemtor noster assumsit, utrumque substantia corporea, utrumque visibile.
latin.394: Addit, pro illustratione Unionis duarum Substantiarum, non item, pro illustratione Modi Unionis, Similitudines: quòd & nos ipsi, inquit, ex corporea & incorporea, ex mortali & immortali substantia sumus compacti; & in Christo divina humanaque natura convenit in unam personam. Vide hanc Epistolam ad Berengarium apud Dacherium in notis ad vitam Lanfranci pag. 24. & 25. Edit. Paris. anno 1648. allegante Otrokocsi in Irenico pag. 79. & 80. Hæc Asceliniana, praesertim cùm Unionem panis & corporis Christi promiscuè inculcent, citra omne discrimen respectûs ad pios & impios, tam genuina sunt modernæ sententiae Lutheranae, quàm Ovum Ovo.

pass_a.391: §. VI. The first Author of the LATTER or SUBTLER CONSUBSTANTIATION is not Berengar — held so by Guitmund from mere uncertainty and another’s report, whom Bayer followed as a blind guide (Disputation on Impanation nos. 15–16); but ASCELINUS, a certain MONK, remembered by William Cave, yet unknown to many, as also to Bayer.
pass_a.392: For Ascelinus, in a Letter to Berengar himself, edited by Dacherius from old membranes of the Abbey of Casale Benedicti, even if he confesses he follows Paschasius’s sentence (namely as far as the corporal presence of Christ’s flesh in the sacrament pertains), nonetheless writes far otherwise than he about consecrated bread and the mode of presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist — defending not Conversion of bread into Christ’s Body, but at least Coexistence of the Body with the blessed bread.
pass_a.393: His words are these: Nor truly ought we to marvel or distrust that God can make this which is consecrated on the Altar (namely bread and wine), by the virtue of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the priest, be UNITED to that body which our Redeemer assumed from the Virgin Mary — both a corporeal substance, both visible.
pass_a.394: He adds similitudes for illustration of the Union of two Substances, not likewise for illustration of the Mode of Union: that we ourselves, he says, are compacted of corporeal and incorporeal, of mortal and immortal substance; and in Christ divine and human nature meet in one person. See this Letter to Berengar in Dacherius’s notes on the life of Lanfranc pp. 24–25 (Paris 1648), cited by Otrokocsi in the Irenicum pp. 79–80. These Ascelinian [sayings], especially since they promiscuously inculcate the Union of bread and Christ’s body without any distinction of regard to the pious and the impious, are as genuine to the modern Lutheran sentence as Egg to Egg.

391: §.VI: first author of the subtler Consubstantiation is not Berengar — Guitmund guessed that from hearsay, and Bayer followed him blind.
It is Ascelinus, a monk Cave remembers and Bayer (with many) never knew.
392: Ascelinus’s letter to Berengar (Dacherius, from Casale Benedicti membranes) owns Paschasius on corporal presence of Christ’s flesh in the sacrament.
On consecrated bread and the mode of presence he writes far otherwise: not conversion of bread into body, but at least coexistence of the Body with the blessed bread.
393: His words: do not marvel that God can make altar-consecrated bread and wine, by Spirit and priest, be united to the body our Redeemer took from Mary.
Both are corporeal substance; both visible.
394: Similitudes illustrate the union of two substances, not the mode: we are compacted of corporeal/incorporeal and mortal/immortal; in Christ divine and human meet in one person.
Letter at Dacherius on Lanfranc (Paris 1648); Otrokocsi cites it.
These Asceliniana — union of bread and body without pious/impious distinction — match modern Lutheran sentence as egg to egg.
